Q: geom_tile() data not displayed in plot that uses Robinson projection centred at 180° A:

When working with spatial data, it is almost always better to ensure all plot objects are spatially referenced. This is especially true when working with non-conformal CRS like the Robinson or Mollweide projections. It helps to avoid issues such as the one you are experiencing.

As well as correcting your st_graticules() code, this solution mimics geom_tile(). It works by first converting your dataframe to a spatially referenced SpatRaster. It is assumed that the coordinates in T_Fe_0.6 are WGS84/EPSG:4326. All of your other code remains the same.

The terra package is used to create the SpatRaster, and the tidyterra::geom_spatraster() function is required to plot the SpatRaster. You will need both these packages for this code to work.

One further consideration is that your T_Fe_0.6 data do not nest 'nicely' up to the extent of the Natural Earth polygons. This ends up leaving white space at certain locations, and around Antarctica in particular. In the case of Antarctica, the Natural Earth data do not include the full extent of the ice shelves, which is where your data appear to stop. I have included an alternate approach that uses a polygon to fill in the background. Omit if the white space is required.

library(rnaturalearth)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(terra)
library(tidyterra)
library(ggplot2)

# Define PROJ4 projection string variable
robin_prj <- "+proj=robin +lon_0=180 +x_0=0 +y_0=0 +ellps=WGS84 +datum=WGS84 +units=m +no_defs"

# st_graticules() object with correctly declared CRS
grat <- st_graticule(
  x = c(0, -90, 360, 90),
  crs = st_crs(4326),
  lon = c(60, 120, 180, 240, 300),
  lat = seq(-90, 90, by = 30)
  ) |> 
  filter(plot12)

# Create SpatRaster version of T_Fe_0.6, WGS84 is assumed
r <- rast(
  T_Fe_0.6[, c("longitude", "latitude", "label")],
  crs = "EPSG:4326"
  )

# Convert numeric 'label' values to strings, which achieves 
# the equivalent of as.factor(label) in your code
r[] <- as.character(r[])

# Create 'background' sf polygon using WGS84 extent,
# then project to robin_prj
bbox <- st_as_sfc(
  st_bbox(c(xmin = 0,
            ymin = -89.99,
            xmax = 359.99,
            ymax = 90),
          crs = 4326)) %>%
  st_segmentize(1e5) %>% 
  st_transform(robin_prj)

# Plot
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = bbox, fill = "lightgrey", color = "lightgrey") +
  geom_spatraster(data = r, aes(fill = label)) +
  scale_fill_discrete(
    name = "Labels",
    na.value = "transparent",
    na.translate = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_sf(data = world, fill = "lightgrey", color = "lightgrey") +
  geom_sf_text(data = labels_x, aes(label = lab), nudge_y = -0.7e6, size = 8) +
  geom_sf_text(data = labels_y, aes(label = lab), nudge_x = -1.5e6, size = 8) +
  geom_sf(data = grat, color = "lightgrey", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_sf(data = border, fill = NA, color = "black", linewidth = 1) +
  theme_void()

For reproducibility, in case the link to the data in the OP goes dead, here's a reprex version of T_Fe_0.6:

T_Fe_0.6 <- data.frame(
  expand.grid(longitude = seq(0.99, 359, length.out = 360),
              latitude = seq(-77, 89, length.out = 118)),
  label = rep(1:4, each = 10620)
  )

Q: Claude Code - Looking for guidance on where to start with coding and tools A:

Good luck getting the hang of programming! Also you asked where a good place to learn would be, I started with the khan academy Java Script course. As for a place to actually start making cool programs try vs code as an IDE(integrated development environment), it's probably the best if you want to be able to program in what ever language you want, but there are specialized IDEs like the Jetbrains IDE IntelliJ that's specifically good for programming java.

Q: Stuck with Gradle Build Running A:

I've run into this issue multiple times and the only thing that worked for me both times was to:

  1. Run ./gradle stop

  2. Open Activity Monitor and end the running java processes

  3. Rerun gradle build

This worked for me on mac

Q: How can I implement a working backend for a login and register page - I've built the frontend A:

I woudnt worry about SQL extensions yet—they’re just for inspecting the database, not building your backend.
Pick a simple stack like Node + Express (or Python Flask) and create /register and /login endpoints.
Use a real database (SQLite is easiest to start), and store passwords hashed with bcrypt—never plain text.
Once it works, you can optionally add a VSCode extension like “SQLTools” just to view/debug your data.
